courses.title: General and Systemic Embryology (ANA 203)
courses.description: Gametogenesis, fertilisation, the first weeks of development, germ-layer derivatives, and development of key organ systems with common congenital anomalies.

topics.title: Gametogenesis and Fertilisation
topics.summary: Spermatogenesis, oogenesis, the ovarian cycle and fertilisation.

material.heading: Gametogenesis
material.body: Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules from puberty: spermatogonia → primary spermatocytes (meiosis I) → secondary spermatocytes (meiosis II) → spermatids → spermatozoa (spermiogenesis); it takes about 64–74 days, and each primary spermatocyte gives four sperm. Oogenesis begins before birth: primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I until puberty; at ovulation the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and completes meiosis only if fertilised. Each primary oocyte yields one ovum and polar bodies.
keyPoints: Primary oocytes arrested in prophase I until puberty
Secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II until fertilisation

material.heading: Fertilisation
material.body: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube within about 24 hours of ovulation. Sperm undergo capacitation in the female tract and the acrosome reaction on contact with the zona pellucida. The cortical (zona) reaction blocks polyspermy. Completion of meiosis II forms the female pronucleus; fusion of pronuclei restores the diploid number and determines chromosomal sex (by the X or Y sperm), producing the zygote.
keyPoints: Site: ampulla of the uterine tube

questions.stem: Fertilisation usually occurs in the:
questions.explanation: The ampulla is the widest and usual site of fertilisation.

questions.stem: Primary oocytes remain arrested until puberty in:
questions.explanation: They pause in the diplotene stage of prophase I.

questions.stem: At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested in:
questions.explanation: It completes meiosis II only at fertilisation.

questions.stem: The block to polyspermy is achieved mainly by the:
questions.explanation: Cortical granules alter the zona pellucida.

questions.stem: The chromosomal sex of the embryo is determined by the:
questions.explanation: The sperm carries either an X or a Y chromosome.

questions.stem: How many spermatozoa arise from one primary spermatocyte?
questions.explanation: Meiosis gives four spermatids, each maturing into a sperm.

questions.stem: Sperm become able to fertilise the ovum after a process in the female tract called:
questions.explanation: Capacitation removes glycoprotein coats from the sperm head.

questions.stem: Spermatids are transformed into spermatozoa by:
questions.explanation: Spermiogenesis is the morphological maturation of spermatids.

topics.title: Cleavage, Implantation and the Bilaminar Disc (Weeks 1–2)
topics.summary: Morula, blastocyst, implantation, trophoblast differentiation and ectopic pregnancy.

material.heading: Week 1
material.body: The zygote undergoes cleavage (mitotic divisions without growth) to form blastomeres; at about 16 cells it is a morula (day 3–4). Fluid enters to form the blastocyst, with an inner cell mass (embryoblast — forms the embryo) and an outer trophoblast (forms the placenta). The blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida and begins implanting in the posterior uterine wall at about day 6–7.

material.heading: Week 2 — 'week of twos'
material.body: The trophoblast forms two layers: the cytotrophoblast and the invasive syncytiotrophoblast, which secretes human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) — the basis of pregnancy tests — maintaining the corpus luteum. The embryoblast forms the bilaminar disc: epiblast and hypoblast. Two cavities form: the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac. Implantation outside the uterine cavity is an ectopic pregnancy, most commonly in the ampulla of the uterine tube; it may rupture and cause life-threatening bleeding. Implantation near the internal os gives placenta praevia.
keyPoints: Commonest ectopic site: ampulla of the tube

questions.stem: A solid ball of about 16 blastomeres is called a:
questions.explanation: The morula forms around day 3–4.

questions.stem: The inner cell mass of the blastocyst forms the:
questions.explanation: The embryoblast gives rise to the embryo proper.

questions.stem: hCG is produced by the:
questions.explanation: The syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG from the second week.

questions.stem: Implantation normally begins at about day:
questions.explanation: The blastocyst starts to implant around day 6–7.

questions.stem: The most common site of ectopic pregnancy is the:
questions.explanation: Most ectopic pregnancies are tubal, usually in the ampulla.

questions.stem: The bilaminar embryonic disc consists of:
questions.explanation: Week 2 forms the epiblast and hypoblast.

questions.stem: Implantation of the blastocyst close to the internal os of the cervix causes:
questions.explanation: The placenta then lies over or near the internal os.

questions.stem: The normal site of implantation is the:
options: Posterior wall of the body of the uterus
Anterior uterine wall near the cervix
questions.explanation: Implantation normally occurs in the posterior wall of the uterine body.

topics.title: Gastrulation, Neurulation and Germ Layer Derivatives (Week 3 onward)
topics.summary: Primitive streak, notochord, neural tube formation and what each germ layer forms.

material.heading: Gastrulation and neurulation
material.body: In week 3 the primitive streak appears on the epiblast, and epiblast cells migrate through it to form the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm (gastrulation). The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube (neurulation); the cranial neuropore closes around day 25 and the caudal neuropore around day 28. Failure of closure causes neural tube defects: anencephaly (cranial) and spina bifida (caudal). Periconceptional folic acid (0.4 mg daily; 4–5 mg if high risk) reduces this risk; raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein suggests an open defect.
keyPoints: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects
Raised AFP → open neural tube defect

material.heading: Germ layer derivatives
material.body: Ectoderm: epidermis, hair, nails, lens, the nervous system (neural tube), and neural crest derivatives (dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, Schwann cells, much of the skull and facial skeleton, odontoblasts). Mesoderm: muscle, bone, cartilage, dermis, heart and blood vessels, blood, kidneys and gonads, adrenal cortex, spleen. Endoderm: epithelial lining of the gut and respiratory tract, liver, pancreas, thyroid and parathyroid glands, urinary bladder epithelium. Somites (paraxial mesoderm) form sclerotome (vertebrae), myotome (muscle) and dermatome (dermis).
keyPoints: Neural crest: ganglia, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, facial skeleton
Endoderm: gut lining, liver, pancreas, thyroid

questions.stem: The process that forms the three germ layers is:
questions.explanation: Gastrulation occurs in week 3 via the primitive streak.

questions.stem: The adrenal medulla is derived from:
questions.explanation: Chromaffin cells arise from neural crest cells.

questions.stem: The epithelial lining of the gut is derived from:
questions.explanation: Endoderm forms the gut and respiratory epithelium.

questions.stem: Spina bifida results from failure of closure of the:
questions.explanation: Failure of caudal neuropore closure causes spina bifida.

questions.stem: Which supplement reduces the risk of neural tube defects?
questions.explanation: Periconceptional folic acid reduces NTD risk substantially.

questions.stem: Skeletal muscle is derived from:
questions.explanation: Myotomes of paraxial mesoderm form skeletal muscle.

questions.stem: Raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein suggests:
questions.explanation: AFP leaks from open neural tube defects into amniotic fluid and maternal blood.

questions.stem: The part of a somite that forms the vertebrae is the:
questions.explanation: Sclerotome cells form vertebrae and ribs.

topics.title: Fetal Membranes, Placenta and Twinning
topics.summary: Chorion, amnion, the placenta and umbilical cord, fetal circulation and twins.

material.heading: Placenta and cord
material.body: The placenta forms from the chorion frondosum (fetal part) and the decidua basalis (maternal part). At term it weighs about 500 g and has 15–20 cotyledons. It exchanges gases and nutrients, excretes waste, produces hormones (hCG, progesterone, oestrogens, human placental lactogen) and transfers IgG antibodies. The umbilical cord normally contains two umbilical arteries (carrying deoxygenated blood from fetus) and one umbilical vein (carrying oxygenated blood to fetus) in Wharton's jelly; a single umbilical artery is associated with other anomalies. Amniotic fluid volume abnormalities: polyhydramnios (e.g. oesophageal atresia, anencephaly) and oligohydramnios (e.g. renal agenesis — Potter sequence).
keyPoints: Polyhydramnios: oesophageal atresia; oligohydramnios: renal agenesis

material.heading: Fetal circulation and twins
material.body: Three shunts bypass the lungs and liver: the ductus venosus (umbilical vein → IVC), the foramen ovale (right atrium → left atrium) and the ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk → aorta). After birth they close to become the ligamentum venosum, fossa ovalis and ligamentum arteriosum; the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres. Dizygotic (fraternal) twins come from two ova and always have two chorions and amnions; monozygotic (identical) twins arise from one zygote, and their membranes depend on when splitting occurs (monochorionic twins risk twin-to-twin transfusion).
keyPoints: Ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus

questions.stem: The normal umbilical cord contains:
questions.explanation: Two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein.

questions.stem: The umbilical vein carries:
questions.explanation: The single vein brings oxygenated blood from the placenta.

questions.stem: After birth, the ductus arteriosus becomes the:
questions.explanation: It closes to form the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: The maternal component of the placenta is the:
questions.explanation: Decidua basalis forms the maternal part.

questions.stem: Oligohydramnios is associated with:
questions.explanation: Without fetal urine, amniotic fluid is scanty (Potter sequence).

questions.stem: Which antibody crosses the placenta?
questions.explanation: IgG is actively transported, giving passive immunity.

questions.stem: Dizygotic twins always have:
questions.explanation: Each zygote forms its own membranes.

questions.stem: The fetal shunt carrying blood from the right to the left atrium is the:
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale shunts blood across the atrial septum.

topics.title: Systemic Development and Congenital Anomalies
topics.summary: Development of the heart, face, gut and urogenital system with common birth defects.

material.heading: Heart and face
material.body: The heart begins beating at about day 22 — the first functioning organ. Septation errors cause congenital heart disease: ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the commonest; atrial septal defects involve the septum primum or secundum; tetralogy of Fallot (pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy) results from anterior displacement of the infundibular septum. The face develops from the frontonasal prominence and paired maxillary and mandibular prominences of the first pharyngeal arch; failure of fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal prominences causes cleft lip, and failure of palatal shelf fusion causes cleft palate.
keyPoints: Tetralogy of Fallot: PS, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH
Cleft lip: maxillary + medial nasal prominences fail to fuse

material.heading: Gut and urogenital system
material.body: The midgut herniates physiologically into the umbilical cord at week 6 and returns by week 10, rotating 270° anticlockwise; failure to return gives an omphalocele (covered by membrane), whereas gastroschisis is a defect beside the umbilicus without a covering. Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline duct ('rule of 2s': 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long). The kidneys develop from the metanephros (ureteric bud + metanephric blastema) and ascend; the fused lower poles of a horseshoe kidney are trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery. Hypospadias is failure of fusion of the urethral folds.
keyPoints: Horseshoe kidney trapped by the IMA
Hypospadias: urethral folds fail to fuse

questions.stem: The commonest congenital heart defect is:
questions.explanation: VSD is the most frequent congenital heart lesion.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a feature of tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation: The fourth feature is right (not left) ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of the:
options: Lateral nasal prominences with each other
questions.explanation: Failure of maxillary and medial nasal prominence fusion causes cleft lip.

questions.stem: Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of the:
questions.explanation: It persists from the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct.

questions.stem: A horseshoe kidney is prevented from ascending by the:
questions.explanation: The fused lower poles catch under the IMA.

questions.stem: An abdominal wall defect with viscera covered by a membrane is:
questions.explanation: Omphalocele is covered by amnion and peritoneum.

questions.stem: The heart starts to beat at about day:
questions.explanation: The primitive heart begins to beat around day 22.

questions.stem: Hypospadias results from failure of fusion of the:
questions.explanation: Incomplete fusion of the urethral folds leaves the urethral opening on the ventral penis.
